title: What If Quantum Could Crack the Energy Transition’s Toughest Problems?
gist: BCG models quantum computing as a 3–7 Gt/year emissions-abatement lever (midpoint ~5 Gt, nearly a tenth of global emissions) concentrated in nine molecular- and materials-simulation use cases across steel, cement, chemicals, trucking, aviation and shipping — while quantum's own footprint stays at ~0.09 Gt in 2040, a roughly 60-to-1 climate benefit ratio. The binding constraint is not computation but physical asset turnover: with steel mills, kilns and chemical plants replaced only every 20–40 years, only ~10–15% of the potential is realizable by 2040, making industrial incumbents that own the assets the likely largest beneficiaries alongside quantum startups.

themes.theme: Quantum's footprint vs. the AI energy panic

insights.claim: Quantum computing is unlikely to repeat AI's energy-demand shock: BCG models the entire global quantum fleet generating roughly 0.09 Gt of CO2e in 2040, less than 0.2% of the expected 50 Gt of global emissions that year.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Investors underwriting power and grid capex on an 'AI-then-quantum' compounding demand thesis should not extrapolate AI's load growth to quantum; the incremental electricity call is immaterial at a system level.
insights.locator: Quantum Computing Could Scale Without an AI-Sized Carbon Footprint

insights.claim: Quantum's projected 2040 emissions equal roughly 7% of potential 2040 data center emissions at the midpoint, making quantum a rounding error next to classical compute's footprint.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Frames relative scale for anyone sizing compute-driven power demand: the data center complex, not quantum, remains the load story through 2040.
insights.locator: Our modeling indicates that quantum computing will generate

insights.claim: The small footprint is a fleet-size effect, not an efficiency effect — a full-scale quantum computer could draw roughly 1 MW, comparable to a small data center, but only about 230 to 1,400 machines are expected to serve global demand by 2040 including spares and government, lab and university machines.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Caps the addressable hardware TAM: quantum is a low-unit-volume, high-value-per-unit business, so hardware vendors' revenue must come from price and service, not fleet scale.
insights.locator: The relatively small footprint is not an indication

insights.claim: More than 11,000 data centers already power AI and other high-performance computing, ranging from roughly 1 MW to 100 MW with some hyperscale facilities approaching 1 GW — infrastructure that quantum is unlikely to need to replicate.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Anchors the AI-versus-quantum infrastructure gap for utilities and real-asset investors evaluating where future compute capex actually lands.
insights.locator: More than 11,000 data centers, ranging in operating requirements

insights.claim: Quantum will be a specialized coprocessor rather than a substitute for classical computing, used only for the narrow set of problems where it has a computational advantage.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Argues against theses that model quantum as displacing classical compute spend; it is additive and niche, which bounds both its revenue and its disruption risk to incumbent semiconductor and cloud franchises.
insights.quote: not as a wholesale replacement for classical computing, but for a specialized set of problems where it can provide a computational advantage
insights.locator: That relatively small fleet reflects how quantum computing

insights.claim: Quantum will not materially increase generative AI emissions because its advantage is in solving different problem types, not in making general-purpose computing cheaper — cutting against the assumption that quantum accelerates the AI compute flywheel.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Deflates the narrative that quantum is an AI-compute accelerant; investors should not price quantum names on AI-adjacency logic.
insights.quote: Nor do we expect quantum to materially increase generative AI emissions, because its advantage lies in solving different types of problems rather than in making general-purpose computing cheaper.
insights.locator: Quantum’s indirect emissions from enabling advances in oil and gas

insights.claim: Quantum's indirect emissions from oil and gas applications are expected to stay limited even as companies explore discovery and optimization use cases, so the rebound-effect objection to quantum's climate case is weak.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Removes a common ESG objection to funding quantum; relevant to sustainability-mandated funds screening the sector.
insights.locator: In oil and gas, companies are exploring early applications

insights.claim: The shift to quantum-safe cryptography could require upgrades to infrastructure such as satellites and fiber networks, but those emissions would be largely one-time rather than recurring.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Flags a discrete capex wave in satellite and fiber network re-encryption that vendors in those verticals could capture.
insights.locator: And while the shift to quantum-safe cryptography could require

themes.theme: Sizing the prize: 3–7 Gt and the 60:1 ratio

insights.claim: Quantum computing could eventually unlock 3 to 7 Gt of annual emissions savings, with a midpoint of roughly 5 Gt equivalent to nearly a tenth of global emissions and roughly 90% of current US emissions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sets the headline number that any quantum-for-climate investment thesis must be measured against — and the range's width (2x) signals how speculative the modeling still is.
insights.quote: We estimate that quantum computing could eventually unlock 3 to 7 gigatons (Gt) of annual emissions savings.
insights.locator: This article is part of a series of publications

insights.claim: Set against roughly 5 Gt of potential annual savings and its own ~0.09 Gt footprint, quantum implies a climate benefit ratio of approximately 60 to 1.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A single defensible ratio for pitching quantum as a net-climate-positive technology to policymakers and impact allocators — a framing AI cannot currently claim.
insights.quote: that level of emissions implies a climate benefit of approximately 60 to 1
insights.locator: Compared with roughly 5 Gt of potential annual emissions savings

insights.claim: Of roughly 50 known quantum computing applications assessed, only 16 could plausibly reduce emissions and just nine offer reductions that classical computing and AI cannot achieve today — seven were discarded because existing technologies like solar PV and electric cars already deliver the same savings.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A screening discipline investors can copy: strip out use cases where classical or existing tech already wins, and quantum's genuine climate moat shrinks from 50 applications to nine.
insights.locator: Where Quantum Could Unlock New Paths to Decarbonization

insights.claim: BCG's model assumes four generations of machines through 2040 with full-scale machines drawing up to approximately 1 MW, producing an estimated 0.001 to 0.15 Gt of CO2e in 2040 from manufacturing and operations combined.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The two-order-of-magnitude spread (0.001 to 0.15 Gt) shows how loosely constrained the hardware roadmap is — a reminder that fleet and power assumptions drive the whole footprint conclusion.
insights.locator: Our Methodology — Emissions Generated

insights.claim: Quantum's emissions come primarily from one-time manufacturing processes tied to building each machine, including the physical qubits required for error correction and expected chip yields, rather than from ongoing operation.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Means the footprint scales with build rate, not utilization — so a faster hardware buildout, not heavier use, is the variable to watch.
insights.locator: These emissions come primarily from one-time manufacturing processes

insights.claim: All nine qualifying quantum climate use cases share one characteristic — they depend on simulating how molecules and materials behave and interact, chiefly by modeling electron interactions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Gives a single filter for evaluating quantum claims: if a pitch is not about electron-level molecular simulation, its climate advantage over classical compute is probably illusory.
insights.locator: These nine use cases share an important characteristic

insights.claim: Accurately modeling even a small molecule would take thousands of years for the largest supercomputers, which is the structural reason classical compute and AI cannot substitute for quantum in catalyst, electrode and sorbent discovery.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: This is the hard technical boundary that makes the quantum-for-materials thesis non-substitutable — the one place where classical scaling genuinely does not close the gap.
insights.quote: The process of accurately modeling a small molecule would take thousands of years for even the largest supercomputers.
insights.locator: Designing a better catalyst, battery electrode, or carbon-capture material

insights.claim: Quantum's contribution is expanding the searchable design space for catalysts, sorbents and compounds rather than producing a single breakthrough — it accelerates screening toward materials with the properties needed for hard-to-abate sectors.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Reframes the value as R&D cycle-time compression, which means the beneficiaries are firms with deep materials pipelines rather than pure-play compute vendors.
insights.locator: Quantum computers are much better at modeling complex interactions

themes.theme: Three flagship applications: capture, molecules, batteries

insights.claim: Direct air capture costs approximately $600 to $1,000 per ton today versus the roughly $100-per-ton level experts cite as necessary for scale adoption — a 6x to 10x cost gap that sorbent chemistry is a major component of.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The explicit cost-curve target for DAC ventures; any DAC investment case should be benchmarked against closing this gap, and sorbent breakthroughs are the identified lever.
insights.locator: Carbon Capture

insights.claim: An effective DAC sorbent must bind CO2 strongly enough to capture it but weakly enough to release it without large energy input, and classical computers can screen known candidates but struggle to evaluate millions of novel complex structures.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Identifies the precise physical trade-off where a quantum advantage would translate directly into DAC opex reduction — a testable milestone for DAC diligence.
insights.locator: Part of that cost involves the materials used to capture CO₂

insights.claim: Ammonia production accounts for approximately 1% to 2% of global emissions and underpins the synthetic fertilizer feeding roughly half the world's population, relying on hydrogen derived largely from natural gas plus extreme temperature and pressure.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Quantifies a concentrated, single-process emissions pool where one catalyst breakthrough could move 1–2% of global emissions — an unusually leveraged target.
insights.locator: Green Hydrogen and Ammonia

insights.claim: The largest gains from unlocking green hydrogen and ammonia come not from lower-carbon production itself but from the downstream industries they help decarbonize, including hydrogen-based steelmaking and lower-carbon shipping fuel.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Value accrues downstream, so investors sizing the hydrogen opportunity should model steel and shipping decarbonization economics rather than hydrogen production margins alone.
insights.quote: The largest gains from unlocking green hydrogen and ammonia come not from lower carbon production itself, but from the downstream industries that they help decarbonize.
insights.locator: These same advances would also make the catalysts

insights.claim: Battery progress is bottlenecked by the combinatorial problem of electrode and electrolyte material selection, where millions of potential configurations are impractical to simulate or physically test — limiting energy storage capacity, lifespan and cost.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Explains why battery improvement has been incremental and where a step-change could come from; watch for quantum-assisted chemistry claims from battery developers as an early signal.
insights.locator: Batteries

insights.claim: Quantum-designed batteries could expand electrification into applications today's batteries cannot serve practically or economically, specifically long-haul trucking and long-duration renewable storage.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Names the two end markets that would re-rate if battery chemistry breaks through: heavy trucking electrification and grid-scale long-duration storage.
insights.locator: Better batteries are critical to several parts of the energy transition

themes.theme: Asset turnover is the binding constraint

insights.claim: Even if quantum delivers the full technical breakthrough, only approximately 10% to 15% of the emissions-savings potential could be realized by 2040 under normal asset-replacement cycles.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The single most important discount factor for any quantum-climate valuation: roughly 85–90% of the value sits beyond 2040, far outside normal investment horizons.
insights.locator: We estimate that industries may realize only approximately 10% to 15%

insights.claim: Steel, cement, chemicals, aluminum, oil and gas, aviation, shipping and trucking are likely to account for roughly 30% of global emissions in 2040, and quantum could eventually abate 20% to 40% of their emissions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Defines exactly which industrial sectors carry the quantum optionality — a sector screen for long-horizon transition portfolios.
insights.locator: Steel, cement, chemicals, aluminum, oil and gas, aviation

insights.claim: Hard-to-abate industries run long-lived capital assets — steel mills, cement kilns, chemical plants and carbon-capture facilities — that may be refurbished or replaced only every 20 to 40 years, so adoption may have to wait for an asset replacement even after a superior material exists.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Capex decisions taken in 2026 lock in emissions for three decades — meaning today's plant rebuild schedules, not quantum milestones, are the leading indicator of when the value lands.
insights.quote: A breakthrough in cement chemistry, for example, may have little near-term impact on a kiln that was rebuilt the previous year and is expected to operate for another 30 years.
insights.locator: But many of these sectors rely on long-lived, capital-intensive assets

insights.claim: Quantum's climate impact will be heavily back-weighted, with physical deployment rather than technological potential determining how rapidly companies capture the opportunity.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The core investable insight: the bottleneck is industrial capex and retrofitting capacity, so engineering, procurement and construction firms may capture value before quantum hardware vendors do.
insights.quote: Quantum’s climate impact is therefore likely to be heavily back-weighted, with physical deployment rather than technological potential determining how rapidly companies can capture the opportunity.
insights.locator: We estimate that industries may realize only approximately 10% to 15%

insights.claim: BCG anchors commercial viability of quantum solutions at around 2035, after which companies still need to translate breakthroughs into industrial-scale processes, build or retrofit infrastructure, and deploy across existing assets.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete date to calibrate quantum roadmap claims against; anything promising industrial climate returns materially before 2035 is running ahead of this model.
insights.locator: Will Quantum’s Benefits Actually Arrive in Time?

insights.claim: Shorter-lived assets such as trucks can adopt quantum-enabled technology far faster than mills and kilns, making trucking the earliest-realizing industrial channel for quantum battery advances.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sequencing signal: fleet-based sectors show the payoff first, so trucking is where to look for the initial evidence that the thesis is working.
insights.locator: Shorter-lived assets such as trucks can adopt new technologies

insights.claim: The 10% to 15% by-2040 figure is deliberately conservative and not a ceiling — compelling economics, government mandates, coordinated global industry standards, retrofit subsidies and greater DAC prioritization could push it higher.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Identifies the policy variables that would convert back-weighted optionality into near-term value — retrofit subsidies and standards are the ones to monitor.
insights.quote: But our 10% to 15% estimate is not a ceiling.
insights.locator: But our 10% to 15% estimate is not a ceiling

insights.claim: Some of quantum's largest potential beneficiaries are industrial incumbents — steelmakers, cement producers and chemical companies — because they already own the physical assets, engineering capabilities and operating infrastructure needed to convert computational breakthroughs into emissions reductions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the pure-play quantum trade: the asset owners, not the technology vendors, may capture most of the value, arguing for exposure to old-economy industrials as a quantum call option.
insights.quote: Some of quantum’s largest potential beneficiaries could be steelmakers, cement producers, chemical companies, and other industrial incumbents that can deploy these solutions at scale.
insights.locator: The investment opportunity is similarly primed for change

insights.claim: The recommended allocation is barbelled — back quantum and materials startups developing the technology while simultaneously directing capital to the established industrial companies that will ultimately deploy it, because funding both accelerates retrofitting and asset replacement.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: An explicit two-sided portfolio construction for the theme, with the second leg (deployers) the one most investors are currently underweight.
insights.quote: Investors could therefore back startups engaged in developing new technologies while also directing capital toward the established industrial companies that will ultimately deploy them.
insights.locator: These companies already own the physical assets

insights.claim: Capital plans, asset-replacement strategies, infrastructure investments and technology partnerships formed today will determine how quickly companies can exploit quantum breakthroughs once viable — making quantum strategically relevant long before the technology matures.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Suggests screening industrial management teams now on whether their capex and partnership posture preserves quantum optionality — a differentiator that will not be visible in financials for a decade.
insights.locator: Business leaders, investors, and policymakers should prepare

insights.claim: IEA STEPS projects renewables growing from roughly 30% of global electricity generation in 2024 to approximately 60% by 2040, while in 2024 renewable curtailment rose approximately 55% to 4% of wind and 3% of solar PV generation.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Curtailment growing 55% in a single year quantifies the storage arbitrage opportunity — the economic gap that better battery chemistry would monetize.
insights.locator: Better Storage Could Accelerate Global Electrification

insights.claim: Longer-duration quantum-enabled batteries would capture otherwise-curtailed renewable electricity and cut fossil-fuel backup reliance, strengthening the case for renewables to take a larger share of the global energy mix.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A second-order threat to peaking gas assets and a tailwind to renewable developers if storage economics break through.
insights.locator: Quantum-enabled advances in battery chemistry could alleviate this problem

insights.claim: Synthetic fertilizer has helped increase crop yields by 30% to 50%, and studies show crop yields could be profitably doubled if fertilizers weren't so expensive — making cheap green ammonia an agricultural productivity story, not just a climate one.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Reframes green ammonia's addressable value around global food output rather than carbon credits, a much larger and more politically durable market.
insights.quote: Studies show that crop yields could be profitably doubled if fertilizers weren't so expensive.
insights.locator: Green Molecules Could Make Food and Energy More Abundant

insights.claim: Fertilizer's dependence on natural gas exposes fertilizer-importing countries to gas price fluctuations and supply shocks, a vulnerability green ammonia would structurally remove.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Links gas price volatility directly to food security in importing nations — a sovereign-risk channel that makes green ammonia a national-security-grade investment for those governments.
insights.locator: But its production depends heavily on natural gas

insights.claim: IEA STEPS projects DAC capturing only about 0.2 Gt of CO2 by 2040, a trivial figure against the EPA's social cost of carbon of roughly $200 per ton in 2023 rising to approximately $300 per ton by 2050.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Once DAC nears $100 per ton, removal becomes cheaper than the societal damage of emitting — a crossover that would re-rate the entire carbon-removal sector.
insights.locator: Affordable Carbon Removal Could Create a Carbon Thermostat

insights.claim: If DAC becomes cheap enough, it could function as a carbon thermostat in which policymakers set a desired climate trajectory and use carbon removal to close the gap, rather than relying on every sector, company and country to abate at source.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A regime-change scenario for climate policy: it would shift the economics from mandates on emitters toward procurement of removal capacity, redirecting where compliance capital flows.
insights.quote: DAC might function as a kind of carbon thermostat: policymakers could set a desired climate trajectory and use carbon removal to narrow the gap between remaining emissions and the reductions required to achieve it.
insights.locator: In a more ambitious scenario

insights.claim: Cheaper DAC would convert decarbonization from a coordination problem across thousands of emitters into a matter of scaling a single technology with increasingly attractive economics, though storage capacity and deployment speed would still gate the pace.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: If this holds, CO2 storage capacity and injection infrastructure become the scarce asset — a chokepoint worth owning.
insights.quote: lower-cost DAC could shift part of decarbonization from being a coordinating challenge across thousands of emitters to being a matter of scaling a technology that possesses increasingly attractive economics
insights.locator: Storage capacity and deployment speed would still determine

insights.claim: Better, cheaper and more transportable batteries could extend electricity access to regions constrained by battery transport difficulty, poor renewable weather conditions or underdeveloped renewable infrastructure, where hundreds of millions of people still lack power.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Points investors toward emerging-market distributed power as the demand pool that unlocks if battery cost and energy density improve materially.
insights.locator: Improvements in battery cost, energy density, and transportability
